How this was built: part numbers, families and descriptions were scraped directly from each brand's own product pages. The Variant column decodes the suffix on each Kenall filename (-TW, -B, -ICT, -NS) — a best-effort read of Kenall's naming convention, not an official key, so double-check anything safety- or spec-critical against the PDF itself. Click a column header to sort, copy next to a filename to copy it, or PDF to open that spec sheet directly from the manufacturer's site. Tap anywhere on a row (or the arrow at its left) to expand its mined technical spec panel. The Filter by mined attribute row above the table gives you three filters: pick any attribute (IP Rating, Mounting Type, CCT, CRI, Dimming Protocol, anything mined) in the first dropdown of a tier, then pick one of the values actually found for it in the second dropdown — all three tiers combine (AND) so you can stack conditions, and the × clears one. Sort by attribute next to Variant sorts the table itself by any mined field (click its ▲ to flip direction). The search box also matches against mined data (try typing "IP65" or "pendant"). Ratings like IP/IK/CCT/CRI are read verbatim off each sheet. A handful of fields would otherwise list hundreds of near-duplicate options, so they're grouped for the dropdown: wattage, lumen output, efficacy, and lumen maintenance into numeric ranges (a family sheet spanning 45-90W matches every wattage band it covers, not just one); mounting type, beam distribution, dimming protocol, UL/ETL/CSA listing, and other certifications into a short list of categories read off each sheet's own wording. Either way, check a row's detail panel for the exact quoted text behind any grouped value. Full methodology, confidence levels, and known gaps are on the Methodology & Known Gaps tab above.

Known Gaps & Assumptions

This guide is a research snapshot, not a live feed from any manufacturer's system. It was built by reading published spec sheets and product pages and modeling their ordering rules by hand (per product, for Kenall). The sections below spell out exactly where the data is solid, where it's a best estimate, and where it's deliberately incomplete — so you can decide what's safe to rely on as-is and what to double-check before using it for a customer-facing or safety-critical decision.

Bottom line: Four of the five Legrand-family brands now have real, footnote-by-footnote modeled configuration counts — Kenall (383 rows), Finelite (89 rows), Focal Point (184 rows), and OCL (90 rows), 746 rows total. Pinnacle remains directory-only (apart from one decoded install booklet, Verbena, added in Rev 19, and Rev 20 adds decoded install sheets for products from three other brands): a 16-product pilot (September 2026) found that 87.5% of piloted Pinnacle spec sheets are brochures with no ordering table at all, confirming the risk described below rather than just theorizing it. The Legrand + Competitors mode adds 29 rows across 3 competitor brand identities (Fail-Safe, Lithonia Lighting, Holophane), all modeled with the same footnote-by-footnote method — see the competitor section below for scope and confidence.

Kenall: how the counts were built, and the 28 low-confidence products

Each of the 292 Kenall products was modeled individually: every field in its ordering-information table, every footnote restriction (voltage/lens/material exclusions, option pairings, mutual exclusions), multiplied out to a real count of valid catalog strings — not a naive "multiply every field" estimate. One product, DFK, had a restriction that only showed up as blanked-out cells in a separate Performance table, not as a footnote at all; that table was used as ground truth instead of the footnotes alone, which is why every product's Performance/dimensional tables were also checked, not just its Ordering Information block.

28 of the 292 products (about 1 in 10) are flagged LOW CONFIDENCE in the underlying model, almost all for the same reason: the spec sheet's Ordering Information table references an external "iMAGINE" image catalog or a "click here for additional configurations" link for one field (usually a lens or image-selection option), and that referenced catalog isn't published in the PDF itself. Where this happens, the field was modeled as a simple binary toggle (standard vs. "custom image") rather than guessing how many actual image options exist behind the link — so these 28 counts are a floor, not a ceiling, on the real number of orderable configurations.

The 28 flagged products: BHRT, CS22, CS24, CS44, CSESL, CSMRI22, CSMRI24, CSMRI44, FNLU6S, FS524, FS548, FS848, HAFD, LPS5, LPSR5, LPS5MRI, LPSR5MRI, MAS813, MAS826, MAS838, MAS850, MCRT, MPCK, MPK6, MRIMAS8, MRS4, RD700, TCD.

Every Kenall configuration count — high- and low-confidence alike — is a count of theoretically valid catalog strings under the published rules. It is not a guarantee that Kenall's factory will accept or stock every one of those combinations.

Finelite, Focal Point, and OCL: how the counts were built (September 2026)

These three brands were modeled the same way as Kenall: each product's own ordering-information table and every footnote restriction (voltage/lens/material exclusions, option pairings, mutual exclusions) read individually and multiplied out to a real count of valid catalog strings — never a naive "multiply every field" estimate. The same check used on Kenall's DFK (a restriction that only showed up as blanked-out cells in a separate Performance/dimensional table, not as a footnote) was applied across all three brands' products too.

The overwhelming majority of rows across all three brands landed LOW CONFIDENCE — 86 of 89 Finelite rows, 172 of 184 Focal Point rows, 85 of 90 OCL rows — for reasons that differ from Kenall's single "iMAGINE catalog" pattern:

  • Continuous dimensions. Many products specify length, stem drop, or overall height as "specify in 1-inch increments up to 208 ft" rather than a discrete list. That field was excluded from the multiplier entirely rather than enumerated (which would inflate the count by a meaningless, arbitrary factor) — so these counts are a floor, not a ceiling.
  • Unpublished option catalogs. Custom RAL/Pantone color programs, "see finish guide" or "see page 3 for full color offering" references, OCL's BIOS SkyBlue light-engine option, and a recurring generic "MOD — modified luminaire, contact factory" escape hatch all point to real options that aren't enumerated in the PDF itself. Each was modeled as a simple binary toggle (standard vs. "custom/other"), the same convention used for Kenall's 28 flagged products.
  • Dense, interacting footnotes. Several products needed their independent-vs-mutually-exclusive fields reconstructed from condensed footnote text. Where that reconstruction required an unverified judgment call, it's flagged and explained in that row's own notes (visible in its detail panel).

A methodology caveat worth knowing: this work was split across 18 separate research passes (one per data batch), each reading its own slice of PDFs independently. They followed the same rules but didn't always make identical judgment calls on ambiguous cases — for example, whether a family of add-on "Factory Options" suffixes can combine freely (modeled as a full power-set in some passes) or should be treated as simple additive toggles (in others). That means two products of similar real-world complexity can land at noticeably different scales not solely because their catalogs differ, but because of which simplifying assumption a given pass applied. Every row's configuration-count notes show the exact arithmetic and every assumption made, so any number can be audited or revised if a specific call looks wrong.

Counts range from 4 (Focal Point's simplest single-variant sconce) up into the hundreds of billions (pendants with many independent color/finish/canopy/control fields) — this spread reflects genuine differences in how configurable these fixtures are, not naive over-multiplication, though the continuous-dimension and unpublished-catalog exclusions above mean even the largest numbers are floors on the true total.

Finelite: 1 product with no orderable matrix. HP-4 Accent Lighting is an MR16 accessory add-on with no independent ordering catalog of its own — just a quantity field and an illuminated/non-illuminated toggle appended to its host luminaire's own order code. Marked N/A rather than guessed.

OCL: 1 PDF fetch failure. AA1 (Atla) could not be fetched after 3 attempts, despite its URL matching OCL's live product page. Marked N/A rather than fabricated.

Pinnacle: pilot results confirm directory-only is the right call (September 2026)

Pinnacle's own ordering guides are not a closed spec. Every family checked — Adeo, Edge, Fina, LiFT, Lucen, and Chute — carries some version of the same disclaimer: "some configurations will not accommodate all voltage/driver/circuiting options; consult with factory," without ever naming which combinations are excluded.

To test whether that risk was as bad in practice as the disclaimer suggests, 16 of Pinnacle's 133 products were piloted across 15 of its 20 families (Edge, Fina, Fina Acoustic, Chute, Loft, LiFT, Cubra, Sorrel, Adeo, Converj, Edge Mini, Linero, Lucen, Traverse, Verbena) before committing to a full run. The result was worse than the disclaimer alone implied: 14 of the 16 piloted source PDFs (87.5%) are brochures or one-pagers with no field-by-field ordering table at all — not a fixable gap, just nothing to count from. The other 2 (Loft 1x1 Direct, Traverse 1x4) did have real order-code tables and were modeled the same way as the other four brands — 326,592 and 107,520 respectively — but both had to be flagged LOW CONFIDENCE for the same unnamed "consult factory" reason, and a naive full multiplication of Traverse's listed fields alone would have landed in the tens of millions before that disclaimer forced the collapse to a binary toggle.

Given a 12.5% yield — and even that yield's two successes are floors, not real ceilings — the decision was to stop at the pilot rather than spend nine more agent passes chasing a mostly-empty result across the remaining 117 products. All 375 Pinnacle rows (133 products) stay directory-only: part number, family, description, PDF link.

Data integrity checks

An automated regression script (validate_catalog.py) runs against the underlying dataset and the built page before every publish. It checks row counts per brand, that every row has a working-shaped PDF link, that Kenall's configuration counts still match the original per-product ledger, that the brand/Legrand logo assets are valid, and that the page's embedded script has no syntax errors. Running it while preparing this tab caught 25 exact-duplicate directory rows (16 OCL, 9 Focal Point) — the same product listed twice because it appeared under two category pages during the original site crawl. Those duplicates have been removed; the brand counts above reflect the corrected totals.

As of the September 2026 configuration-count expansion, the script also checks: that every Finelite/Focal Point/OCL row's configuration count (where present) matches that brand's own source ledger exactly; that every configuration count is either a positive integer or one of the documented "N/A" strings, never a malformed value; and that Pinnacle rows still carry no configuration count, since that brand stayed directory-only by design.

Link verification

All ~1,121 PDF links were captured by reading each manufacturer's site directly, but this Claude environment has no outbound network access to kenall.com, pinnacle-ltg.com, finelite.com, focalpointlights.com, or ocl.com, so the links could not be live-tested from here. They're well-formed URLs pointing at each manufacturer's own document host, but a manufacturer can move or rename a file at any time. Spot-check a sample before distributing this guide widely, especially for anything customer-facing.

Data currency

This is a point-in-time snapshot. Manufacturers revise spec sheets, retire SKUs, and reorganize their sites on their own schedule, and there's no automatic refresh built into this page — treat it as current as of when it was built, not as a live catalog.

Brand & Legrand logo assets

The Kenall, Pinnacle, Finelite, Focal Point, OCL, and Legrand marks shown throughout this guide were supplied directly as image files and cropped for display here. They haven't been separately checked against each brand's current logo/style guidelines, so if a brand refreshes its mark, this page's copy won't update on its own.

September 2026: configuration-count expansion to Finelite, Focal Point, and OCL

Following an earlier technical-attribute-mining pass across all 5 brands, the same per-product combinatorial modeling used for Kenall was extended to Finelite (89 rows), Focal Point (184 rows), and OCL (90 rows) — 363 more rows, bringing the total with real configuration counts to 746 across four brands. Pinnacle was piloted on 16 of its 133 products first rather than committing to a full run; the pilot's 87.5% "no ordering matrix" rate confirmed the brand should stay directory-only (full detail in the Pinnacle section above). See the "Finelite, Focal Point, and OCL: how the counts were built" section above for the full methodology, the confidence breakdown, and an important caveat about consistency across the 18 separate research passes this work was split into.

Competitor data (Legrand + Competitors mode): scope, sourcing, and confidence

The Legrand + Competitors toggle adds 29 rows across three competitor brand identities, all belonging to two much larger corporate parents. Scope was deliberately narrowed to only the product lines that directly compete with Kenall's correctional and cleanroom categories — not Cooper Lighting Solutions' or Acuity Brands' full catalogs, which run to thousands of SKUs across dozens of brands unrelated to this guide's purpose:

  • Fail-Safe (a Cooper Lighting Solutions / Signify brand) — 22 rows: 18 correctional/high-abuse products (FMS, FMR, FMB, FCC, FCT, FSR, FUSL, EXL, FSP, FSN, FCZ, ENV/ENW/ENC, HVSL2, HVSL4, HVSL8/12, HVL8/12, FVS4, FVS8) plus 4 cleanroom products (CFA, CLP, CLM, FLR/FLR2).
  • Lithonia Lighting (an Acuity Brands brand) — 1 row: the SRTL/2SRTL cleanroom troffer family, modeled as a single combined row since both widths share one unified option set and differ mainly in which physical sizes each can form.
  • Holophane (an Acuity Brands brand) — 6 rows: the full "Confinement Series" correctional lineup (HLCMP, HLRMP, HLRMQ, HLSMP, HLSMQ, HLWMP), confirmed complete via three independent sources.

Consciously excluded as out of scope (found during research, not modeled because they aren't true correctional/cleanroom competitors to Kenall): Gotham Lighting's EVOR cleanroom downlights (4 SKUs, an Acuity brand adjacent to but distinct from Lithonia/Holophane) and Holophane's 11 general-purpose outdoor/perimeter products (cobra heads, floodlights, wallpacks) — the latter are marketing-adjacent to "Holophane" as a name but aren't correctional luminaires. Also excluded: 5 discontinued Fail-Safe cleanroom products (CFS, CFDFA, CFE-4, CRS, CFSLP), all superseded by the CLM/CLP rows already in this guide.

Confidence: all 29 competitor rows are flagged LOW confidence — none reached the HIGH bar (a fully closed, unambiguous ordering table with zero interpretive judgment calls). 22 rows had a fully fetched, readable spec-sheet PDF (fetch_status: OK); 7 rows (CLM, and all 6 Holophane products) rest on a partial or indirect source read (fetch_status: PARTIAL) because the primary spec-sheet PDF either resisted transcription or returned unparseable binary content on every fetch attempt, and the row was built instead from the manufacturer's own rendered product page and/or a corroborating third-party spec aggregator. Every row's own confidence notes spell out the exact arithmetic and every interpretive call, the same audit standard used for Kenall/Finelite/Focal Point/OCL.

Weakest rows, flagged explicitly rather than smoothed over:

  • HLRMQ (Holophane) — no manufacturer product page or spec-sheet PDF could be located at all; every figure comes from a single third-party aggregator. The weakest row in the entire competitor set.
  • HLSMQ (Holophane) and HLRMQ both show only two lumen values (1,200 / 1,911 lm) attached to an identical ~28.8W wattage figure — a pattern that may really be one continuous output range mis-modeled as two discrete SKUs rather than a genuine two-code table.
  • HLCMP (Holophane) — two sources gave conflicting lumen-tier structures (a 3-tier reading tied to housing length vs. a 9-value discrete list); the 3-tier reading was used for its coherent physical basis, but this is an unresolved source conflict, not a confirmed fact.
  • CLM (Fail-Safe) — its own spec-sheet PDF could not be reliably transcribed page-by-page, so this row rests on a secondary, lower-fidelity read of Cooper's product page; its field cardinalities are plausibly an undercount relative to its close sibling CLP, which shares the same LD4 platform and was read directly.

Methodology is otherwise identical to the Legrand-family brands: every table on the actual spec sheet was read (not just the page labeled "Ordering Information"), continuous dimensions (cut-to-length, "specify in 1″ increments") were excluded from the multiplier entirely rather than enumerated, cross-field footnote restrictions were enumerated jointly rather than approximated as flat percentages, and unpublished/external option catalogs (custom RAL colors, "consult factory," a JS-only web configurator) were modeled as a simple binary toggle. Counts range from 80 (Holophane HLRMQ, a floor on a weakly-sourced row) to just over 2.14 billion (Fail-Safe HVSL8/12, whose large independent architectural-finish and decorative-band catalogs stack combinatorially) — the same kind of genuine configurability spread already seen across the Legrand-family brands, not over-multiplication.

As with the rest of this guide, competitor PDF links were captured once during research (this environment has no persistent outbound network access for live re-testing), so treat them the same way as the Legrand-family links: well-formed at time of capture, not guaranteed to still resolve.

October 2026: first decoded Pinnacle install sheet (Verbena)

Every other Pinnacle Install Sheets row (129 of 133) is still a link to the manufacturer's PDF with no contents read; the Documents column marks these Link only. Four rows (Verbena 3, Verbena 3 Alternating Joint, Verbena 4, Verbena 4 Alternating Joint) now carry Decoded FEB2025, meaning the booklet Verbena_Installation.pdf (12 pages, footer Verbena_Booklet_FEB2025) was read page by page and its mounting content was transcribed by hand. Those four rows share one PDF, so this is 1 of the 43 unique Pinnacle install PDFs.

What was decoded: mount methods (CAC cable power side and non-power side, wall and surface brackets), items the booklet marks as supplied by others, the page 12 installation disclaimers, the CAC and wall/surface spacing tables, and mount-point rules. These appear in the expanded detail panel of every Verbena row and in the Install Lookup tab.

What was not decoded: connector footprint dimensions (90, 120, 135 degree corners, Y, T, X), remote driver box procedures (page 11), and lens removal and installation (page 12). The Install Lookup tab and detail panel point to those pages in the PDF instead.

Derived values, not printed in the booklet:

  • CAC mount points per fixture (2 for spacing A, 3 for spacing B) are read from the page 2 diagram. The table itself gives spacing only. Run totals apply the booklet's rule: all mounting points on the first fixture, all but the first on each later fixture.
  • Wall and surface bracket totals (2 on the first or independent fixture, 1 on each later fixture) come straight from the table headings. The note that Dim A equals fixture length minus 12 in, and Dim B equals fixture length, is a pattern that holds for all 7 printed rows, not a stated rule.

Known quirks in the source: the Y, T, and X connector pages reuse the corner wording ("attach corner to first fixture"). The booklet does not say who supplies the J-box for wall or surface mounts, or the fasteners for the wall brackets, so those are listed as not stated rather than assumed. Page 3 says hands-free hanging applies only to wall mounting, and that ceiling mounting needs two people.

Confidence: table values were cross-checked against the PDF's extracted text and the diagram. Treat them as MEDIUM-HIGH confidence for planning, and confirm against the PDF (or with Pinnacle) before ordering or specifying.

October 2026: one row per product, and four more decoded install sheets (Rev 20)

Row layout. Pinnacle used to have up to three rows per product (Spec Sheet, Install Sheets, Brochure). Rev 20 merges them into one row per product, so Pinnacle goes from 375 rows to 133. Every row now has a Documents column with a separate button per PDF: Spec, Install, and (Pinnacle only) Brochure. Nothing was dropped, and all 375 original Pinnacle links are still there as buttons. The PDF count in the page header now counts unique linked PDFs instead of rows, so it no longer matches the earlier 1,121 figure.

Install sheets added from other brands. Five PDFs supplied for review were read and transcribed by hand. Each is attached to the rows it names and shows a mounting methods table, a hardware table (part numbers where the sheet gives them, and who supplies each item), cautions, and the gaps in the sheet.

Status badges. Current means the manufacturer's own page linked the sheet when the links were captured (Kenall and Finelite), or the sheet is dated 2026 and filed under a 2026 folder on the manufacturer's site (Finelite HP-1). Archived means the manufacturer lists it under previous installation instructions, so a newer sheet may exist. Uploaded copy means the sheet came from a file supplied for review and its manufacturer link and listing status were not checked. A dashed Install button means no download link is on file.

Row matching is by the sheet's title, and part of it is inference. The flange frame sheet is titled for the AMB/ME/MEP series, so it is attached to all three; the Kenall MEP page was the only page checked for it. ME11MRI is not named on it and is left unattached. The Polina sheet covers the unlit wall-mount versions (AUPOLC-SHXS-27-WM and -42-WM) only, but it is attached to the AUPOLC row as the closest match. HP-2 WW-D has its own current Finelite sheet (see Rev 21 below), so it is not attached to the HP-2 Direct sheet.

What "Not stated" means. In the hardware tables, "Provided" and "By others" repeat the sheet's own wording. "Not stated" means the sheet is silent, and it is not a guess. The Kenall MEP and flange frame sheets, for example, never say who supplies the eyebolts, washers, screws, or nails.

What was not decoded. The Polina sheet's step drawings (pages 2 and 3) have no text, and its dimension callouts could not be read reliably, so only the bracket orientation rule and the component key are in the guide. Apart from these five sheets and the Verbena booklet, no install PDF contents have been read. Links for Kenall, Finelite, OCL and Focal Point install sheets were added in Revs 21 and 22 (below).

Types and status. Install sheets get the button. Replacement and service sheets (driver, light engine, addenda, troubleshooting, quick start), mitered corner sheets, and accessories (GridBox, caddy, labels, end caps) are listed in the row detail only. Current means the file was linked from the manufacturer's current product or downloads page when the script ran (Kenall product pages, Finelite Downloads, OCL product pages). Listed (Focal Point) means the file appears in Focal Point's site map; that is not a statement that it is the latest revision. Archived means it came from Finelite's previous installation instructions page, so a newer sheet may exist. Archived sheets are labelled "(old)" and sort after current ones.

How rows were matched, and where it is inference.

  • Kenall: by the product code in the file name and the product page the file was found on. Each file is attached to every table row with that code (for example the three HPG14 sheets all attach to HPG14). The log records only the first page a shared file was found on, so a sheet that serves several products can be missing from the others. Several matches come from the page name rather than the file name (for example IC100 to MEIC, FLAIR to HAFD, DL4 to BHDL4), so confirm the model on the PDF.
  • Finelite: by the series and mount named in the file name. The HP-1 and HP-2 rows were checked against the Finelite Downloads table. Everything else follows the file name. Files named for two or three series (for example HP-2-4-6) are attached to each series they name. Replacement sheets for engines and drivers are attached to every row of the series they name, and wall wash (WW) rows get the WW-specific ones. The Arm mount sheet (HP-24) is attached to the HP-2 and HP-4 ID, D and I rows because its name covers both series. The Finelite HP-2 WW-D row now has its own current sheet.
  • Focal Point: by the model code in the file name (for example FSM4LS_IS0518 attaches to the FSM4LS row). Compound codes such as FSM2L-CXF only take sheets that name the whole code. The suffix after the model (G, TF, NF, XF, SM and similar) is shown in the button label as written on the file, and its meaning is not decoded here. Where the site map listed two files with the same IS number, only the one with the higher revision suffix is linked, which assumes a higher suffix is newer. Sheets named for several models (for example ASM1S_ASM2S) attach to each row named. The FSDL sheets attach to both Skydome LED rows because the file names do not say which. The ID+ module and trim sheets (LC4_LC44 and similar) attach to all four rows of that family.
  • OCL: by the file name and the product page it was found on. A file named for a product (for example Cirque-Install.zip) is attached to every row of that family, because only the first page that linked it is recorded. Sheets named by mount code (for example UA1-S1SA) are attached only to the rows with that mount type. Allure, Newport and Intrigue share one ZIP, as do Element and Vapor, and Ola, Hela and Cosma share the Printz ZIP and care sheet.

The Finelite TCS and FineTune files are controls, not luminaires, and have no guide rows.
